`healthtrends` produces health trend reports based on
[Health Trends in England](https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/static-reports/health-trends-in-england/England/overview.htm): a set of accessible HTML pages summarising public health indicators. Reports can be produced for England, its statistical regions and upper tier local authorities. It pulls indicator data from the
[Fingertips API](https://fingertips.phe.org.uk/), applies the project's
selection and quality rules, and renders the report with Quarto.

This vignette walks through the pipeline end to end:

1. `import_healthtrends_files()` — set up the working directory.
2. `set_header()` — brand the report (optional).
3. `get_data()` — fetch and save the indicator data.
4. `generate_reports()` — render the HTML report.

```{r setup}
library(healthtrends)
```


## The workflow at a glance

The shortest path to a full report is three calls. `generate_reports()` fetches
the data for you when `refresh_data = TRUE`, so you do not have to call
`get_data()` yourself:

```{r glance}
import_healthtrends_files()

set_header(
  title   = "Health Trends in England",
  org     = "Department of Health & Social Care",
  org_url = "https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/department-of-health-and-social-care"
)

generate_reports(
  area_codes   = c("E92000001", "E12000004"), # England + East Midlands
  refresh_data = TRUE
)
```

The rest of this vignette explains each step and when you would call
`get_data()` on its own.


## 1. Set up the working directory

`import_healthtrends_files()` creates the folder structure the report needs and
copies in the Quarto templates, CSS and configuration supplied with the package.
**Run it first** — the other functions expect these folders to be present.

```{r import}
import_healthtrends_files()
```

It creates three folders at the top level of your working directory:

* `healthtrendsfiles/` — the Quarto templates and styling.
* `input/` — a copy of `config.yaml` (used to reach the Fingertips API).
* `output/` — where the saved dataset and the finished HTML report are
  written.

The `overwrite` argument (default `TRUE`) controls whether the package's own
template files are refreshed. Use `overwrite = FALSE` to keep any local edits
you have made inside `healthtrendsfiles/`:

```{r import-nooverwrite}
import_healthtrends_files(overwrite = FALSE)
```

If you call it with `overwrite = FALSE` before the folder exists, it stops and
tells you to run it with `overwrite = TRUE` first.


## 2. Brand the report

`set_header()` sets the title, organisation name, organisation link and logo
shown in the report header. It edits the header template inside
`healthtrendsfiles/`, so it must be run **after** `import_healthtrends_files()` —
otherwise it stops with a message asking you to import the files first.

```{r header}
set_header(
  title     = "Health Trends in England",
  org       = "Department of Health & Social Care",
  org_url   = "https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/department-of-health-and-social-care",
  logo_path = "input/logo.svg"
)
```

Each argument is optional and only the ones you supply are changed; anything you
leave as `NULL` keeps its placeholder default. A few notes:

* `logo_path` points at an image file on disk. It is copied into the report's
  `www/` folder for you, so you do not need to move it manually. Leave it `NULL`
  to keep the placeholder logo.

You only need to run `set_header()` again if the branding changes; the edited
header persists in `healthtrendsfiles/` between report runs.


## 3. Fetch the data

`get_data()` downloads the indicator data from Fingertips, applies the project's
quality checks (minimum number of time points, missing-value thresholds and
regional completeness) and saves the result as a `.rds` file in the output
folder (`output_path` in the config file, `output/` by default). It also
returns the data frame, so you can inspect it.

```{r get-data}
htie_data <- get_data(
  area_codes = c("E92000001", "E12000004") # England + East Midlands
)
```

Key points:

* **England is always included.** `E92000001` is added automatically if you
  leave it out, because every indicator is benchmarked against England.
* **Supported areas.** Only 2023 upper tier local authorities (codes starting
  `E06`, `E08`, `E09` or `E10`) and statistical regions (codes starting `E12`)
  are supported. See *Choosing area codes* below.
* `data_name` sets the output file name (default `"health_trends_data.rds"`).
  Use a different name to keep a test dataset separate from the main one.
* `generate_urls = FALSE` skips building the Fingertips link columns (they are
  created but left as `NA`). This is noticeably faster and is handy when you are
  only testing the data step.

```{r get-data-test}
# A quicker run for testing: custom file name, no link columns
get_data(
  area_codes    = "E12000004",
  data_name     = "test_data.rds",
  generate_urls = FALSE
)
```

You usually do not need to call `get_data()` directly.
`generate_reports(refresh_data = TRUE)` calls it for you. Call it on its own when
you want to refresh or inspect the dataset without rendering the report — for
example, to check which indicators survived the quality filters before running a
full render.


## 4. Render the report

`generate_reports()` renders the summary and detail pages to `output/` with
Quarto. It reads the configuration named by `config_file` (default
`"input/config.yaml"`, the copy `import_healthtrends_files()` puts in place).

```{r generate}
generate_reports(
  area_codes   = c("E92000001", "E12000004"),
  refresh_data = TRUE,
  config_file  = "input/config.yaml"
)
```

The `refresh_data` argument decides where the data comes from:

* `refresh_data = TRUE` (default) refreshes the dataset from the API first, by
  calling `get_data()` internally. Use this for a normal run.
* `refresh_data = FALSE` reuses the existing `.rds` already saved in the
  output folder. This is faster and works offline, but stops with an error if
  no dataset has been created yet.

```{r generate-nofetch}
# Re-render from the data already on disk, without hitting the API
generate_reports(
  area_codes   = c("E92000001", "E12000004"),
  refresh_data = FALSE
)
```

If you call `generate_reports()` with no `area_codes`, it defaults to England
plus the nine statistical regions.


## Choosing area codes

`area_codes` takes 9-character ONS codes. Supported prefixes are:

| Prefix                | Area type                          |
|-----------------------|------------------------------------|
| `E92`                 | England (added automatically)      |
| `E12`                 | Statistical region                 |
| `E06`, `E08`, `E09`, `E10` | Upper tier local authority (2023 boundaries) |

Two things to watch for:

* **Combined areas.** A few areas are usually reported combined with a
  neighbour in Fingertips rather than on their own — Isles of Scilly (with
  Cornwall) and City of London (with Hackney). `generate_reports()` detects
  these and tells you which code to use instead.
* **Superseded codes.** Older Barnsley and Sheffield codes are corrected
  automatically to the codes Fingertips currently holds, so either version works.
